title: A Layman Thinks About AI

reader_summary.headline: Howard Marks explains why investing in artificial intelligence is extremely difficult and uncertain.
reader_summary.overview: Howard Marks argues that while AI is a major global development, it is hard to predict which companies will succeed. He notes that the technology changes too fast and that we do not fully understand how AI systems work inside. Investors must accept uncertainty and focus on price rather than trying to guess future profits.

key_points.text: Investing in AI is hard because many unpredictable factors must align correctly for a strategy to succeed.
key_points.evidence_quote: An investor in AI has to be at least somewhat right about the evolution of the technology, the demand for compute, the competitive structure, the beneficiaries of the technology, the availability of the technology, the availability of financing, and the timing of all the above.

key_points.text: We built AI systems that act like minds, but we still do not fully understand how they actually work inside.
key_points.evidence_quote: We know what AI is made of and how it was built, almost perfectly, but we know surprisingly little about how it actually does what it does.

key_points.text: The economy relies too heavily on a few AI companies, creating risk if their massive debt causes interest rates to rise.
key_points.evidence_quote: AI-related debt issuance has totaled nearly $600 billion globally so far this year, according to Goldman Sachs, comprising debt issued by the hyper-scalers in data center slash project financings and by other AI-linked borrowers.

notes: In his latest memo, Howard Marks, Co-Chair of Oaktree and Chair of Brookfield's Investment Solutions Group, revisits the topic of artificial intelligence, describing it as both deeply consequential and highly unpredictable. He addresses 11 questions that surround investing in AI, including who will profit and what it means for the credit markets. Howard points out that while these questions can’t be answered definitively, the presence of uncertainty doesn’t mean investors can or should ignore AI: it’s simply too important for that.
transcript:
This is the memo by Howard Marks.
A. Layman thinks about AI.
Should we invest in artificial intelligence, and can we do so, intelligently?
That's what I'm going to address in this memo.
On one hand, I'm not a tech person, and I don't claim to have above-average knowledge of artificial intelligence,
or technology investing, for that matter.
On the other, AI is the biggest development of our time, and could be one of the most impactful things the world
has ever seen. So investors don't have the option to abstain from thinking about it.
With that disclaimer, I'm going to share my deliberations, put forth the questions I'm wrestling
with, not all of which are directly relevant to investing in AI, and provide my thinking about
them. While my limited knowledge prevents me from definitively answering these questions,
I hope to provide a service by assembling them in one place. And while news on AI comes hot
and heavy these days, with security prices for AI and AI-adjacent companies
up and down. I'm not going to try to keep up, since what I have to say relates to the long-term
outlook for AI, not what security prices will be tomorrow. Investing consists of just one thing, positioning
capital to benefit from future events, and most investors cope by relying on forecasts.
But not everything is equally predictable, and not all forecasters are equally skilled.
Thus, to invest in AI based on expectations about the future, and I think that's all we have,
we must consider both what we think the future may hold and the chance we can get it
right.
I've written in the past about the fact that people who engage in top-down investing have to be right
about the outlook for the economy, the industry, the company, and the market.
If they have a 60% probability of getting each one right, which is probably generous,
what's the probability of getting all four right? The answer is 13%, 0.6 to the 4th
power, assuming the outcomes are independent of each other. In the case of AI, there
an unusually large number of important variables, each of which complicates the
decision of how to invest. An investor in AI has to be at least somewhat right about
the evolution of the technology, the demand for compute, the competitive structure, the beneficiaries of the
technology, the availability of the technology, the availability of financing, and the timing of all the
above. Assessing these key elements seems to me to be unusually challenging. In that case,
what's the combined probability that any thesis is correct? That's just
something to think about as you listen.
Lastly, bear in mind that A, we can never know everything about an investment.
B, the biggest mistakes are made when people think they do, and C, the incompleteness of our knowledge
regarding the future can't be permitted to completely prevent us from taking action.
It's the investor's job to bear risk in the pursuit of profit.
How much and in what form are decisions we each must make.
But, given its vast potential, we can't decline to participate in AI just because
the future is unclear.
Question 1. How does AI do what it does? Before getting more granular, I'm going to start with a big-picture,
non-financial question that I find particularly interesting.
Since I have absolutely no knowledge on this subject, I went to Anthropics Claude for some
answers. Here's some of what it said.
We know what AI is made of and how it was built, almost perfectly, but we know surprisingly
little about how it actually does what it does.
We also know the training recipe. Show it enormous amounts of text, have it guess the next word,
and nudge billions of internal settings slightly each time it guesses wrong. Repeat that trillions of
times. Nobody wrote the rules for how it answers the question.
Those rules emerged from the nudging, spread across billions of numbers that mean
nothing individually. The best phrase I know for this is that these systems are grown rather than
designed. Researchers in interpretability are making real progress. They have found, for example, that a
model writing a rhyming poem picks the rhyme word before it writes the line, which means
which means it plans ahead. But they can explain only explain only small
slices of what goes on. It's like having a complete record of every trade in the market
and still not knowing why prices moved. When I explain how I reached an answer, research suggests my
explanation doesn't always match what actually happened inside. A model asked how it
did a sum may describe the school book method while internally doing something very different.
So the honest summary is that we've built a mind-like thing we can
inspect completely and still can't fully explain. And when it explains itself, it may be no
more reliable than we are when we explain ourselves. Interestingly, here Claude talks like it's a person. As
you think about answering the questions that follow, consider these. Does anyone truly understand
how AI works? How will AI evolve and what will it be able to do and when? How will
users put it to work? What impact will it have on users' profitability?
Investors may not have to know all these things, but it's my understanding that few people have significant
insight into these matters. If that's the case, can anyone reliably answer the questions that follow?
Question 2. What will AI be able to do? What AI is great at is evolving. Just a few years ago, what
AI could do was generally summed up as knowing everything that has occurred before,
identifying historical patterns, extrapolating them, and using this ability to perform tasks. This has
already made huge changes in some areas, like coding, and promises to alter many aspects of life as we
presently know it. But now, AI has gone well beyond that to something that probably can fairly
be described as reasoning. Just this one area poses several questions that are both
stimulating and daunting. AI's full potential will be subject to the answers to some of these. Can AI's process
be made to reflect our preferences, values, and goals, or will it apply its own? Can AI be depended on to
be honest, humble, ethical, and loyal? Will it be accurate, an objective, or subject
to influence, and manipulation? Will it admit when it's wrong or doesn't know an answer? Can it give us
skepticism rather than sycophancy? Will it become a threat to humans and seek to advance its own interests
instead of ours? How will it do in areas such as creativity, originality, aesthetics,
subjectivity and intuition? Will it be able to perform what I call second-level thinking?
Thinking in a way that's different from that of most people and at a higher level, leading to superior
solutions? Will it be able to think about the future and blue sky to the same degree as humans? Can
it be instructed to furnish primary sources, as opposed to published citations, and provide
counter-arguments? Will one model be able to do it all? Or will different models be best
at different things? If so, how will we know which one to use? Will artificial general intelligence? Will artificial
general intelligence, the ability to do everything a human can do, be the standard? Will A-G-I, mean the ability
to do the same things as A, the average person, B, a person in the 90th percentile,
or C, the smartest person in the world? In other words, will there be varying levels of knowledge
and things AI doesn't know? All these things bear on what work will be entrusted to AI.

As Warren Buffett pointed out about the Internet during the tech bubble,

We know AI will increase efficiency, but will it increase profitability? And whose? If several AI

R.O.I be ground down? In which case the economic benefits may go more to the users of AI than

With what degree of certainty? How strong are the motes surrounding today's leaders?
Perhaps the most startling characteristic of AI is the speed at which it makes progress.
In that connection, I'm struck by the fact that today's leading model labs, open AI and Anthropic,

If it's possible, consider the vast resources and potential of the so-called hyperscalers,
Amazon, Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta, and Oracle. Who will win among these incumbents?
or will it be companies we've never heard of? How about companies that don't
exist yet? Think about the probability 20 to 25 years ago that the leaders then

ask, what's the probability today's AI leaders will still be the leaders in five or
10 years? If the competitive picture can shift, as I suggest, how much
is a stake in today's leader's worth.
Question 5. How profitable will the companies be?
The value investor estimates a company's earnings or cash flows in the future,
discounts them back to the present, and compares the result with today's stock price.
To predict earnings in the future, we need answers to questions like these.
How many units of its product will it sell?
What will be the selling price per unit?
What will each unit cost to produce?
How much of the profit will need to be reinvested in developing the next product?
What will be the company's resulting return on investment?

What will its product be capable of doing, and how will customers put it to work?
Will the product be priced as a commodity, or a unique, a unique, essential good?
How long will chips last, and how fast will data center depreciation have to be charged off?
For how long will today's break-neck spending race continue?
Will enough money be made to produce a decent return on today's capital expenditures?
I could certainly be wrong, but I don't remember puzzling over uncertainties of this magnitude
in my days analyzing the conglomerates in the 1970s or in connection with the Internet and e-commerce in 1999 to 2000.
Those businesses, as novel and complex as they were,
simple and straightforward compared to AI. So I wonder, can we project 20-30 earnings for
today's hypers and leading frontier labs, let alone companies that mostly consist of conjecture? Do we have to be able
to predict earnings reasonably accurately to invest? If we come up with estimates, how much confidence
should we have in them? And if we can't, how can we think about investing in AI companies?
Here's the test I propose nowadays.
Tell me what you think the EPS for a given AI company will be in five years.
Will you bet that the eventual answer will be within plus or minus 50% of your figure?
For example, if you guess $10 per share, how confident are you that the actual figure
will be between $5 and $15?

Historically, data centers were digital warehouses that stored data and hosted computer

workplaces of AI. Analogous to auto plants there where AI is produced, ranging from storing information
and training models to providing time on the system, called compute.
Data centers are a critical element in the development of the AI industry.
A construction of data centers, and thus the performing of compute is subject to constraints,
physical, and otherwise.
While the future of AI is exciting, some people might prefer to take a cautious approach to participating
participating in it.
This suggests investment via tangible infrastructure, rather than developers and vendors of

find opportunities that are insulated from the uncertainties just listed
and won't be subject to overbuilding and thus oversupply of compute.
As in all forms of investing, there will be successful data center investors and less successful

Question 11. How should one think about investing in AI?
I consider artificial intelligence the most consequential and least predictable development for investors
